short: An earthquake is strong shaking of the ground when rocks suddenly slip along a crack.
more: Earth's outer layer is broken into giant puzzle pieces called tectonic plates.
The plates drift very slowly, and that pushing builds up stress in the rock.
When the stress gets too big, the rock suddenly slips along cracks called faults.
A sudden slip at a fault sends shaking waves out, and that shaking is the earthquake.

q: Can scientists tell when an earthquake is coming?
short: Not yet. No scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake.
more: Scientists use instruments called seismometers to measure the shaking waves.
That tells them when and where a quake happened, and how strong it was.
They can't name the day, but they can work out the chances of a big quake over years.

q: What is a volcano, and why does it erupt?
short: A volcano is an opening where hot melted rock from deep inside escapes to the surface.
more: Underground, melted rock is called magma. Once it reaches the surface, we call it lava.
Magma can rise where the plates of Earth's crust slowly pull apart.
It also rises where plates push together and one slides under the other, deep into the hot Earth, where it melts.
It can also rise at hot spots, where heated magma is lighter and floats upward.
Earth is not alone: Venus and Mars are covered with volcanoes too, and scientists are still checking whether any on Venus are active.

short: There are about 1,350 volcanoes around the world that could erupt again, not counting long volcano chains on the ocean floor.
more: About 500 of them have erupted since people began writing history down.
Many more volcanoes sit hidden along the ocean floor.
More than 80 percent of Earth's surface, above and below the sea, was made by volcanoes.

q: Why does the Moon change shape?
short: The Moon doesn't really change shape; we just see different amounts of its sunny side.
more: The Moon makes no light of its own. Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off it.
As the Moon circles Earth, we see more or less of its lit-up half.
It takes about 29.5 days to go from one new moon to the next.

q: Why is the Moon covered in holes?
short: Those holes are craters, made when space rocks crashed into the Moon long ago.
more: The Moon has no air, so it has no wind or weather to wear craters away.
Once something hits the Moon, the mark stays, frozen in time.
Earth gets hit too, but weather, water, plants and volcanoes slowly erase or bury our craters.

q: What is the space station, and how fast does it go?
short: It's a home for astronauts that circles Earth 16 times every day.
more: The space station zooms along at five miles every second.
It is almost as long as an American football field, end zones included.
People have lived on board, nonstop, since November 2000.

q: Can I see the space station from my backyard?
short: Yes! It looks like a very bright star gliding across the night sky.
more: It has no flashing lights and does not change direction, so it's not an airplane.
It moves much faster than a plane.
Look within a few hours of sunrise or sunset, when sunlight shines on it against a dark sky.

q: How far away is the nearest star?
short: Our nearest star is the Sun! The next closest, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.25 light-years away.
more: A light-year is how far light travels in one Earth year.
Light zips along at about 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometres) every second.
Even so, sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us.
One light-year is about 6 trillion miles (9 trillion kilometres).

q: What is the farthest thing people ever sent into space?
short: NASA's Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object.
more: It was sent to fly past the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn.
In August 2012, it crossed into interstellar space, the space between the stars.
NASA worked out that it would reach one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026: as far as light travels in a whole day, about 16 billion miles (26 billion km).

short: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity that builds up inside a storm cloud.
more: Strong winds in the cloud lift water drops up and push ice down.
Where they bump past each other, electric charges get stripped off and build up.
When the charge gets strong enough, it jumps out as a flash of lightning.
Lightning can be about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

short: Hurricanes grow over warm ocean water near the equator, fed by warm, wet rising air.
more: The rising air lowers the pressure below, which pulls in even more air.
The middle of the storm, called the eye, is calm and clear.
In some places, people call these storms typhoons or cyclones instead.
Weather satellites about 22,300 miles up watch them to help warn people.

q: Why is there ice at the poles?
short: The poles stay so cold that snow piles up year after year instead of melting.
more: Because Earth is tilted, each pole spends part of the year in darkness.
Even in summer, sunlight hits the poles at a low slant, so it is spread thin and warms the ground less.
Snow that doesn't melt builds up over thousands of years into thick ice sheets.
Sea ice is frozen ocean water. It grows in winter and shrinks in summer.
Snowy sea ice bounces most sunlight back to space, which helps it stay cold.

q: Why is ice at the poles melting?
short: Earth is getting warmer because the air is trapping too much heat, like a greenhouse.
more: At night, the atmosphere holds onto heat instead of letting it escape to space.
Over tens of years, a few degrees of warming starts causing changes.
Ice is melting near the North and South Poles. When ice on land, like the giant ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, melts into the ocean, the sea level rises.
Sea ice is already floating, so when it melts it does not raise the sea level much at all.

short: Many birds fly south to find food, then fly back north to raise their babies.
more: As fall turns to winter, plants and insects get harder to find.
So birds travel to warmer places where food stays plentiful.
In spring, they return to find a mate, build a nest and raise their young.
The Arctic tern flies more than 70,000 kilometres (about 44,000 miles) a year, from pole to pole!

q: Do whales go on long trips too?
short: Yes! Humpback whales have one of the longest migrations of any mammal.
more: They feed in cold oceans that are full of food.
Then they swim to warm, shallow waters to have their babies.
Some swim 5,000 miles (8,000 km) between those places.
Humpbacks can swim from Alaska to Hawaii, 3,000 miles (4,800 km), in as few as 28 days.
